1:
The first line is a textual crux, and they divide over whose heart is meant. Adam Clarke says it is hard to make sense of as it stands — how can the transgression of the wicked speak within my heart? — and reports that four of Kennicott’s and De Rossi’s manuscripts read his heart instead of mine, a reading supported by the Latin, Greek, Syriac and Arabic, which he thinks should be adopted. It is not by example that such a person sins, for the fountain of the impure streams is in his own heart. Charles Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by a longer road. The literal rendering is an utterance of sin to the wicked within my heart; and since to the wicked cannot mean concerning the wicked, the only possible sense as it stands is that sin speaks to me, the wicked man, in my heart. But the psalmist must have written in his heart, since all the ancient versions except the Chaldee followed that reading — and this gives a very fine sense: sin is personified as the evil counsellor sitting in the heart of the wicked, so that sin is his oracle and conscience is on the wrong side.

The others keep the received text and make the psalmist the one concluding. John Gill is careful to say that the transgression of the wicked was not really in him — sin was, and sin of the same kind — but that taking notice of the wicked man’s daring impieties he concluded in his own mind what follows. Matthew Henry has him conclude that there is no fear of God before that man’s eyes, since if there were he would not dare break God’s laws. John Wesley puts it in a sentence: considering the transgressions of ungodly men, I conclude they have cast off all fear of the divine majesty. C.H. Spurgeon generalises: men’s sins have a voice to godly ears and are the outer index of an inner evil, so that unholiness is clear evidence of ungodliness and wickedness the fruit of an atheistic root. He must be a desperate traitor, he adds, who rebels in the monarch’s own halls.

What occasion produced the psalm is disputed too. Adam Clarke reports that the Syriac and Arabic suppose it composed during Saul’s persecution, while Calmet places it in the Babylonish captivity. John Calvin dissents from what he says almost all interpreters suppose, that David is expressing wonder at God’s goodness in bearing with the wicked who contemn him. His own opinion is different: the prophet, harassed by ungodly men, first complains of their depravity and then takes refuge in the goodness of God, to console himself in the assurance that he shall at length be delivered — as the conclusion shows, where he fortifies himself by reflecting that he is safe under God’s protection. Keil and Delitzsch decline to look for an occasion: the psalm belongs to a group in which David complains of the moral corruption of his generation, reflections of the age rather than of particular occurrences. None of them can account for the title styling David the servant of the Lord, used nowhere else but in one other psalm.

Augustine of Hippo reads the opening not of one man but of a race of ungodly men, who fight against their own selves by not understanding — not because they cannot, but because they will not. So it is when men love their own sins and hate God’s commandments: the Word of God is your adversary if you are a friend to your ungodliness, and your friend if you are its adversary. And of the finding out of iniquity he says the man wrought so as not to find it, for there are men who seem to seek their iniquity and fear to find it, because once found they are told to depart from it.
5:
Matthew Henry marks the turn as deliberate relief. Having looked round with grief on the wickedness of the wicked, David looks up with comfort on the goodness of God, a subject as delightful as the former was distasteful; seeing the world polluted and God dishonoured, he turns to God and says, however it be, yet thou art good. Among men we often complain that there is no truth nor mercy, but all these are in God without the least alloy: whatever is amiss in the world, nothing is amiss in him who governs it.

C.H. Spurgeon works the same image as a sky. Mercy is like the ethereal blue, a canopy for all earth’s creatures, surmounting the loftiest peaks of human provocation; clear sky is evermore above, and mercy calmly smiles over the din and smoke of this poor world. When we can measure the heavens, then shall we bound the mercy of the Lord; and afflictions are like clouds, but the divine truthfulness is all around them. Adam Clarke makes the point morally: God is infinite in mercy, else such transgressors must be cut off at once, but his long-suffering is meant to lead them to repentance, and his faithfulness binds him to keep the promises his mercy made. John Wesley puts the pair as infinite and incomprehensible, the faithfulness covering both God’s threatenings and his promises.

John Gill canvasses several senses: the general mercy the earth is full of, which reaches up to the heavens as men’s sins do; or special mercy, whose seat is the heart of God; or its origin, heaven being, as some Jewish interpreters say, the fountain of mercy. Charles Ellicott keeps to the rendering: to the heavens reacheth thy grace, thy faithfulness to the sky — there are no narrower bounds of divine mercy and truth.

The mountains of the next verse draw the closest attention. Adam Clarke takes the phrase literally as mountains of God, what in the present language of geology would be called primitive mountains, formed at the beginning and not by earthquake or inundation as secondary and alluvial mountains are supposed to be; and the great deep he makes the great abyss, as incomprehensible as the chaos of Genesis 1:2. John Gill explains the epithet as one of excellency, like the cedars of God, and reports Gussetius’s view that the highest mountains are the pillars of God’s palace. Charles Ellicott says the epithet implies not only greatness but a reference to God as Creator, as the rain too is called God’s brook, and takes the deep for the abyss of waters of which the seas were the surface. He sets the comparison beside Wordsworth’s two voices, one of the sea and one of the mountains — where the modern poet hears Liberty, the ancient Hebrew heard Righteousness, the strength of the hills becoming an emblem of God’s eternal truth and the sea’s expanse of his justice. John Wesley compresses it: steadfast and unmoveable; the judgments unsearchable as the ocean; the care extending to the worst of men and to the brute beasts.

Adam Clarke ends by quoting the Old Psalter, which paraphrases the mountains of God as righteous men — spiritual hills of God, because they are high in contemplation and sooner receive the light of Christ. The metaphor is taken from mountain tops first catching the rising sun, and he calls it a very fine thought, much beyond the rudeness of the times in which that Psalter was written. Of the closing clause he asks whether God takes care of cattle, and answers that he appoints the lions their food and will certainly provide for the poor of his people. John Gill takes the righteousness either of God’s government of the world, as unreachable as high mountains yet as immovable, or of that by which he justifies sinners, visible in the gospel and lasting as the hills.
7:
The exclamation is taken as a question no one expects answered. Adam Clarke says it is asked in the way of admiration, but that no answer is looked for from angels or men, the lovingkindness being indescribably excellent, abundant and free. Charles Ellicott would render the adjective precious rather than excellent, and replaces the therefore of the second clause with a simple conjunction: and sons of men, they find shelter. John Wesley makes the same comparison among the attributes — though all of them are excellent, mercy is above all most excellent, or precious and amiable. John Gill lists what makes it so: it has appeared to men and not angels, and to some and not others, reaching the chief of sinners, and all of God’s sovereign good pleasure, there being nothing in them that could move him to it.

The shelter Adam Clarke divides in two. The children of Adam trust God’s providence for their bodies and his mercy for their souls, and these are the two wings of the divine goodness under which they take refuge; the allusion, he suggests, may be to the cherubim above the mercy-seat.

What the house is, and what its fatness, divides the next verse. John Gill makes the house the church of God, and the fatness the provisions there — the word and ordinances, and especially Christ himself, the bread of life, making a feast of fat things which those who trust in the Lord are welcome to eat and drink of abundantly. Charles Ellicott denies that fatness here means the fat of the sacrificial offerings: it is the stream of grace flowing from above to enrich men as rain enriches the earth, and the house may be the whole earth, as Gesenius took it, or more probably heaven. To preserve the parallelism he renders the verb literally, they shall drink to the full, and sets beside the verse Keats’s endless fountain of immortal drink, pouring to us from the heaven’s brink. Adam Clarke reports the same versions, saturated as a thirsty field is by showers from heaven, inebriated in the Latin, and drunken of the plenteousness of thy house in the Old Psalter’s northern English. John Wesley takes the fatness of the delightful provisions God has prepared in heaven, and the river as denoting both their plenty and their perpetuity.

Adam Clarke then presses a reading no one else offers. The Hebrew behind the river of thy pleasures he takes as the river of thy Eden, noting that four manuscripts spell the word so; the promise is therefore a restoration to their paradisaical estate, with reference to the river that went out of Eden to water the garden at Genesis 2:10. Alternatively the temple, and under it the Christian church, may be compared to Eden.
9:
The fountain is read at three depths. John Gill makes God himself the fountain of living waters, not only of natural life but of spiritual life, the soul being quickened when dead in sin, and of eternal life besides. The phrase denotes, he says, that life is originally in God as in its fountain and that he is free in communicating it. John Wesley says the same in a line: it is in God as in a fountain and from him derived to us, and that endless life alone is worthy of the name.

Adam Clarke begins conventionally and then turns somewhere no one else goes. In Scripture phrase the words may signify a spring, such as the Jews called living water to distinguish it from ponds and reservoirs fed from the clouds or by pipes. But there seems to him a higher allusion, since the Hebrew reads, with thee is the vein of lives. Does this not allude, he asks, to the great aorta, which, receiving the blood from the heart, distributes it by the arteries to every part of the body, whence it is conducted back again by the veins? As the heart distributes blood to the remotest parts, so God by Christ Jesus conveys the streams of his providential goodness to all the worlds he has created, and the influences of his grace to every soul that has sinned.

Of the second clause Adam Clarke notes that the metaphor changes, God being now compared to the sun in the firmament: no man can illuminate his own soul, and all understanding must come from above. Charles Ellicott would render it by thy light rather than in thy light, and says this wonderful verse inspired Milton’s invocation to the author of all being, fountain of light, himself invisible amid the glorious brightness where he sits. It contains, he adds, the germ of that teaching which had its highest development in the Epistles of St John — though the original intention seems to be that God’s favour commends itself as divine in origin, especially to those in the covenant. John Wesley hears the repetition as deliberate: light in the first clause is light discovering, in the second light discovered or enjoyed — the light of God’s presence, fully manifested when we see him face to face.

The petition that follows is noticed for its verb. Adam Clarke renders it literally, draw out thy mercy, the allusion to the spring being still kept up. John Gill reads the same word the same way, draw out thy lovingkindness to a greater length, and is careful about what is asked: the love of God itself always continues, though its manifestations are not always the same, so the request regards the open discovery of it. He is careful too about those prayed for, whose knowledge and faith and love are not the cause of God’s love but only point out its objects. Adam Clarke glosses the same phrases briefly — those who acknowledge God in a crooked generation, and the straight of heart, who have but one end in view.

C.H. Spurgeon reads the prayer as modest and well-founded at once: we ask no more than a continuance of past mercy, that the Lord would extend this grace to all the days of all who have been taught to know his faithful love. This prayer, he says, is the heart of the believer asking precisely what the heart of his God is prepared to grant, and it is well when the petition is but the reflection of the promise. The worst thing to be feared by the man of God is to be forsaken of heaven, which is why the prayer is made; but the fear is groundless. And he draws the lesson that although a continuance of mercy is guaranteed in the covenant, we are still to make it a matter of prayer.
11:
The two figures of the petition are distinguished. Charles Ellicott notes that the one tramples on the lowly and the other is full of violence, and would render the second verb expel rather than remove — though we have no indication from where, unless from the temple. Adam Clarke gives the same verb as shake me, or cause me to wander. John Wesley identifies the foot as that of proud and insolent enemies, coming so as to overthrow him. John Gill looks for a person: some proud enemy such as Ahithophel, of whom R. Obadiah expounds it, who lifted up his heel against David; and the words are applicable to any haughty enemy of Christ and his people, and particularly to antichrist, who exalts himself above all that is called God.

Adam Clarke refers both verses to the captivity. The Jews, compared with the Babylonians, were the people that knew God; and the psalmist prays against the treatment they had received through the seventy years, asking to be restored to their own land and never removed from it. The fall of the last verse he takes accordingly: there, in Babylon, are the workers of iniquity fallen. He reads it as a prophecy of the destruction of the Babylonish empire by Cyrus, and points to the sequel — that the empire was destroyed is historical fact, that its people never recovered their liberty is also fact, and that Babylon is now blotted out of the map, its site no longer known, is confirmed by every traveller who has passed through those regions.

He then sets out how differently the fathers read that one word there. Augustine referred it to the pride of the preceding verse: there, in or by pride, do all sinners perish. Jerome placed it in heaven, where the evil angels fell through pride, and others in paradise, where our first parents fell through pride and disobedience; Eusebius put it in hell, whither the proud and disobedient angels were precipitated; and others made it the point at which persecutors, by pride, brought God’s judgments on themselves. Clarke reports the whole catalogue and dismisses it in a sentence: the first interpretation is the best.

Charles Ellicott takes the word as one of place and leaves it there: the poet has some definite incident in mind, but has not told us enough to identify it. John Gill offers two possibilities, either the pit they dug for others or hell itself, where they shall be turned at last. C.H. Spurgeon makes the scene present to faith: faith sees them scattered on the plain, and before our very eyes sin, death and hell lie prostrate. Jesus has already thrown all the foes of his people on their faces, and in due time all sinners shall find it so; for the defeat of the ungodly is final, total and irretrievable. However high the powers of darkness may carry it at present, the time hastens on when God shall give evil such a fall as shall for ever crush the hopes of hell.
